summary.text: Eggs should be cooked until the yolk and white are firm; raw or undercooked eggs carry a foodborne illness risk.

selection.text: Fresh eggs make the best-looking fried eggs, with a compact oval shape, thick white and high yolk.
Use very fresh eggs for poaching.

storage.text: Refrigerated raw shell eggs keep with little quality loss for about 4 to 5 weeks past the pack date.
After you bring them home, raw shell eggs keep about 3 weeks.
Hard-boiled eggs in the shell keep up to one week refrigerated.
Leftover egg whites keep up to 4 days in a covered container.
Store yolks covered in the refrigerator and use them within a day or 2.
Refrigerate egg-containing leftovers promptly and eat them within 2 to 3 days.

preparation.text: Refrigerate eggs for a week to 10 days before hard-boiling, which makes them easier to peel.

substitutions.name: Pasteurized shell eggs or pasteurized egg products
substitutions.note: For recipes that use raw or lightly cooked egg, the Egg Board suggests pasteurized shell eggs or pasteurized egg products.

substitutions.name: Pasteurized egg whites (not a foaming substitute)
substitutions.note: The Egg Board says egg white from pasteurized shell eggs and liquid egg white products will not whip properly in foaming applications.

safety.text: Raw or undercooked eggs can increase foodborne illness risk, especially for people with certain medical conditions.
Over-easy, poached, sunny-side-up and soft-boiled eggs may not reach a food-safe temperature.
Cook casseroles and other egg-containing dishes to at least 160°F.
Keep shell eggs and egg dishes at 40°F or below when not being cooked or eaten.

why.text: Scrambling is a versatile breakfast choice.

steps.text: Beat the eggs with milk, salt and pepper until blended.
Heat oil in a nonstick skillet over medium heat, then pour in the egg mixture.
Pull, lift and fold the eggs as they set until thickened with no visible liquid egg.
Remove from heat as soon as they are thickened, since the pan keeps cooking them.

tips.text: Avoid cast iron, which can turn scrambled eggs greenish.

doneness.text: Cook until thickened with no visible liquid egg.

methods.label: Fried eggs in a nonstick skillet

why.text: Choose fried eggs for sandwiches or to top steak, burgers or hash, as the Egg Board suggests.

steps.text: Heat 2 tsp oil in a nonstick skillet over medium-high heat until hot.
Slip in the eggs one at a time, then reduce the heat to low.
Cook slowly until the whites are set and the yolks begin to thicken but are not hard.
Slide a turner under each egg and flip it to cook the second side to your liking.

tips.text: Soft-yolk eggs may not be safe for high-risk people; for them, cook until the yolk is firm.
Keep the heat moderate; high heat makes eggs tough and rubbery.
For basted eggs, use 2 tbsp butter and cover the pan between bastings.

doneness.text: Cook to 160°F held for 2 minutes; the Egg Board says a fried egg cooked to that guideline has a firm yolk.

why.text: Poached eggs suit light meals on toast or English muffins, per the Egg Board.

steps.text: Heat 2 to 3 inches of water to a boil, then lower the heat to keep it gently simmering.
Break each egg into a cup, then slip it into the water.
Cook 3 to 5 minutes until the whites are set and the yolks just thicken.

tips.text: Soft-yolk poached eggs may not be safe for high-risk people; for them, cook until the yolk is firm.
Do not swirl the water; keep it quietly simmering.
Vinegar or salt in the water is not necessary and can flavor the eggs.

doneness.text: Whites fully set and yolks thickened but not hard.

why.text: Hard-boiled eggs make a grab-and-go snack, so a batch can be cooked ahead for the week.

quantities.label: Standing time by egg size (large 12, medium 9, extra large 15)

steps.text: Place the eggs in a single layer in a saucepan.
Add cold water to cover the eggs by 1 inch, then heat until boiling.
Remove from heat, cover, and let stand about 12 minutes for large eggs.
Cool completely under cold running water or in ice water, then refrigerate.

tips.text: Eggs cooked too long or at too high a temperature can get a greenish ring around the yolk.
Hard-boiled eggs peel most easily right after cooling.

doneness.text: Eggs should be fully set and thoroughly cooked; hard-boiled eggs spoil faster than raw eggs.

why.text: Oven baking fits casseroles, quiches and stratas, which the Egg Board lists as bake-to-temperature egg dishes.

steps.text: Bake until a thermometer at the center reads at least 160°F and holds it for 2 minutes.
Check several spots, because hot spots and oven swings cause uneven cooking.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly and eat them within 2 to 3 days.

tips.text: Most baked egg dishes reach 160°F for 2 minutes by the time they are done.

doneness.text: Bake until the center holds at least 160°F for 2 minutes.
